vignette:
Fatima describes her life before as having a certain rhythm, a predictability that she took for granted. Mornings in her home country were marked by the smell of baking bread from the corner shop and the distant call to prayer. Her life was contained within the familiar streets of her neighborhood, her marriage to Omar, and the weekly ritual of going to the open-air market. It was there, on a Tuesday that felt like any other, that the rhythm of her life was shattered.

She was haggling with Mr. Hakim, the fruit vendor whose kindness was as well-known as the sweetness of his figs. He was weighing her purchase, his back to the street, when the world dissolved into a deafening roar and a flash of white-hot light. Fatima was thrown backward by the force of the blast, her ears ringing with a sudden, profound silence. When she pushed herself up from the dusty ground, the vibrant colors of the market had been replaced by a monochrome of gray dust and black smoke. The air was thick with a smell she has never been able to name, a coppery, burnt odor that still catches in the back of her throat at unexpected moments. She saw Mr. Hakim, and the image of what the blast had done to his familiar, kind form is a permanent fixture behind her eyes, ready to project itself onto her vision without warning.

In the chaotic months that followed, she and Omar made the decision to leave. The journey was a blur of fear and paperwork, but they arrived in the U.S. with a shared, unspoken hope that a new place would mean a new beginning. They settled in a rural agricultural community, and Fatima found work in the vast fields, a landscape so different from the crowded city she had left behind.

At first, the physical labor was a relief. The burn in her muscles and the sheer exhaustion at the end of the day were a welcome distraction. But the relief was temporary. The open fields, which should have felt safe, began to feel exposed and threatening. A tractor backfiring a quarter-mile away sends her diving to the ground, her heart pounding with a terror that is utterly disconnected from her reality. The drone of a small crop-dusting plane overhead can trigger a full-blown panic, forcing her to hide between rows of tomato plants until the sky is quiet again.

Her life has shrunk. She works, and she goes home to her small, sparsely furnished apartment. Omar is gone now. He left two years ago, unable to understand the woman he was now married to—a woman who flinched at his touch, who stared through him with vacant eyes, and who would erupt in sudden, inexplicable rage over a dropped glass or a question asked at the wrong time. Fatima doesn't blame him. She feels like a ghost in her own life, watching herself go through the motions. The woman who once laughed with vendors at the market is a stranger to her.

She avoids anything that reminds her of that day. She cannot go to the local farmer's market, the sight of brightly colored produce piled high on tables is unbearable. She drives five miles out of her way to avoid a construction site. The joy she once found in cooking has vanished; the smell of certain spices can transport her back to the market square just before the explosion, and the memory is so vivid, so complete, that she has to grip the counter to keep from collapsing. At night, sleep offers no respite. She jolts awake from nightmares of dust and screaming, her body drenched in sweat, the phantom smell of smoke filling her apartment. She then lies awake for hours, staring at the ceiling, feeling a profound and unshakable guilt for having simply been buying fruit at the wrong time.
